One, the whole grid is one point, the center, two values per input would take two to the hundredth points. Since Metropolis and Ulam's 1949 paper, The standard tool has been random points, like this one. How far off would a million random points land? Start with two inputs. Our function is one inside this quarter disk, zero outside. Its average is exactly one-half. A 10 by 10 grid puts 52 of its 100 points inside, two points off. 100 random darts put 44 inside, six points off. In two dimensions, the grid wins. Now give each a million points and add inputs. The disk becomes a ball, grown to cover exactly half the box. The grid's million points give each axis a thousand values in two dimensions, then a hundred, ten, three. From 20 dimensions on, just the center inside the ball. So the grid says the ball fills the box, 50 points off. Even two values on 19 axes is 18 points off, while the darts stay under a tenth of a point. Maybe darts win by giving every axis more values. One flip is either zero or one. Its average is a half, so every flip misses by exactly a half. Repeat the 100 dart experiment 300 times. In both, the estimates spread this wide. Those misses fall up or down at random, so they partly cancel. 16 darts stray about 4 halves, not 16. N darts stray about root n halves. Divide by n, and the typical miss is a half over root n. For 100 darts, 5 points. We measured 4.8. Any other function swaps the half for its own spread, sigma, there's still no d. So back to our ball, a million darts any dimension. How far off is a typical estimate? One half over a thousand, five hundredths of a point.
